title: Composite quantum geometry of superconductors
authors: Florian Simon, Thomas Bernat, Annica M. Black-Schaffer
abstract: The interplay of superconductivity and the quantum geometry of the normal state has recently been the subject of an array of studies, especially regarding the superfluid weight. In this work, we turn our attention to the quantum geometry of the superconducting state itself, set by the Bogoliubov-de Gennes (BdG) Hamiltonian, which dictates the geometric and topological properties of superconductivity. We show that under three general conditions, namely superconducting fitness, orbital uniformity of the superconducting pairing, and absence of normal-state spin-flip terms, the BdG quantum geometry exactly separates into a sum of the normal-state quantum geometry and an additional pairing quantum geometry, thereby displaying a simple composite structure. We show that this separation holds for all spin-singlet and -triplet pairings, including nonunitary spin-triplet pairing. We further provide explicit analytical formulas for the pairing quantum geometry for all these cases. These results establish how superconducting pairing alone easily drives both topology and a finite quantum metric, thus being present even in topological trivial or flat band superconductors, with no normal state quantum geometry. To complement these results, we also derive the BdG quantum geometry of a general two-orbital spin-singlet superconductor with non-uniform pairing and finite superconducting fitness. Here, our explicit analytical results establish a non-separable composite BdG quantum geometry, with the normal state and pairing contributions generally intertwining, thereby producing even more possibilities for finite quantum geometry. Our results provide design rules for creating superconductors and superconducting hybrid structures with nontrivial topology and finite quantum metric and will additionally help in the experimental diagnosis of unconventional superconductivity.
summary: This paper analyzes the quantum geometry of superconducting states using the BdG Hamiltonian. It shows that under specific physical conditions, this complex geometry cleanly separates into contributions from the normal metal and the superconducting pairing itself. This provides powerful theoretical tools for designing or diagnosing superconductors with engineered topological properties.
main_problem: The study investigates the quantum geometry of the superconducting state, defined by the Bogoliubov-de Gennes (BdG) Hamiltonian, to determine when this geometry can be decomposed into independent normal-state and pairing contributions.
main_result: Under specific conditions—superconducting fitness, orbital uniformity of pairing, and absence of normal-state spin-flip terms—the BdG quantum geometry cleanly separates into a sum of the normal-state and pairing quantum geometries.
method: The authors use analytical derivations based on the BdG Hamiltonian formalism to calculate the Quantum Geometric Tensor (QGT) for various superconducting pairings (singlet and triplet).
model_or_system: The system is superconductors modeled by the Bogoliubov-de Gennes (BdG) Hamiltonian, generalized to multiorbital structures. The analysis covers spin-singlet, spin-triplet, and nonunitary pairing states.
key_observables: The BdG quantum geometry, which includes both the quantum metric and Berry curvature; separability of this geometry into normal-state and pairing components.
important_parameters: Superconducting fitness ($\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{k})$), orbital uniformity of the superconducting pairing, and the nature of the pairing (spin-singlet vs. spin-triplet).
main_assumptions: The clean separation of the quantum geometry requires meeting three general conditions: superconducting fitness, orbital uniformity of the pairing, and absence of normal-state spin-flip terms.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the multiorbital BdG framework, derives the separability results for various pairings under ideal conditions, examines non-separable cases where contributions intertwine, and concludes with design rules for engineered superconductors.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous geometric framework to diagnose unconventional superconductivity by quantifying how pairing interactions alone can generate topological features or finite quantum metrics, even when the normal state is trivial.
